reading.identification: 't Galgenhuisje, Groentenmarkt 5, Ghent: a late-17th/18th-century one-room-deep infill house wedged against the Groot Vleeshuis, in use as a café since 1776 and known as the smallest café in the city.
reading.notes: Identification is solid, facade parameters are not. In set B the building is occluded by a Denys construction hoarding, a white picket fence and scaffolding; the magenta box mostly encloses the printed banner, whose text ("'t Galgenhuisje ... het kleinste cafe van Gent. Sinds 1776") is what identifies the target. Set A is a degraded 3D-tile mesh with no resolvable storey lines or openings. Hence every field is marked inferred; nothing here supports a 'seen'. Height 9.0 m has height_source=no-data, so I have distributed it rather than trusted it as measured: ground 3.2 m + upper 2.9 m gives a 6.1 m eaves, with the gable apex at 9.0 m (~53 deg pitch over the 4.3 m frontage). The gable is turned end-on to the square, which is both the Ghent vernacular and the only way 9 m of height sits sensibly on a 2.6 m depth; a ridge parallel to the street would need a ~63 deg pitch. 'marble' in the trim slot is a dielectric proxy for Balegem limestone (plinth, sills, door surround) - the enum has no limestone class. roughness_mm 3 carries the brick bond and mortar joints as a scattering term, per the 1-10 cm regime; do not mesh them. Geometry budget belongs on the window reveals, the stone sills, the gable cornice and the gable steps of the silhouette, and on the cafe threshold at eye level. Scene context: fronting street is pedestrian with car_access=none, so no parked or moving vehicles - the classic failure here would be lining Groentenmarkt with cars. Populate instead with cafe terrace furniture at the door, the construction hoarding line, bins, bikes, and wet paving_stones as seen in set B.

reading.identification: Late-18th to early-19th-century Ghent burgher house with a white lime-rendered Louis XVI/Empire classicist front over an older market-square core, three storeys under a slate roof, now in commercial use as a Europabank branch on the Groentenmarkt/Pensmarkt corner.
reading.notes:
SCALE: image scale fixed at ~29.8 px/m by matching the measured cornice-to-ground run (y195-600, 405 px) against the recorded 16.9 m height; implies camera ~27 m out, i.e. across Groentenmarkt. All metric reads below use that scale.

SEEN (set A supports these): three window rows resolve as distinct dark bands with heads at y=255, 360, 490 -> 3 storeys, matching building:levels=3. Row pitch is 105 px (3.5 m) between the two upper rows and 130 px (4.35 m) between first and ground, so the ground floor is genuinely taller, as expected for a commercial/bank frontage. Five window columns resolve on the outlined frontage at centres x=390/454/516/574/630, spacing 64->56 px with foreshortening to the right, mean 2.08 m. 5 x 2.08 = 10.4 m, which reproduces frontage_width_m independently - the bay count and the cadastre agree, so I am confident in 5 rather than 6. A 6th axis cannot be excluded behind the tree at x>660 but nothing in the roofline suggests it. The wall reads as a uniform light rendered surface with no brick modulation, corroborating building:material=plaster; the roof reads slate-grey with the ridge running parallel to the street.

INFERRED, and why: window dimensions are at the edge of what the plate supports (dark runs ~30 px wide, ~65 px tall -> ~1.0 x 2.2 m including reveal shadow smear), so I set 1.15 x 2.1 m, a 1.83 aspect, which is the standard Ghent Louis XVI proportion. Reveal and glazing bars are far below 25 cm/texel: rendered masonry of this period sets sashes back behind a plaster surround, hence shallow (~0.12 m), and the T-division survives on almost all Ghent refrontings even where the joinery is modern.

ROOF FORM: the tiles actually read closer to hipped - there is a slope at the left end - but the tile roof is a low-poly blob and OSM says gabled, so I have taken the data and marked the whole group inferred rather than claim I saw a gable. Ridge-parallel-to-street IS legible, but I could not split the evidence flag within the group, so the conservative mark governs.

GROUND FLOOR: heavily compromised - a horizontal tile-texture seam runs across at y=470-490, a tree occludes from x=660, and market clutter fills the base. Tall dark openings are present across the frontage, which is all I can honestly say; shopfront is the class inference from amenity=bank on a market square (a modern glazed branch frontage with signage), not an observation. Institutional_portal was rejected: Europabank branches do not have monumental doorways.

LEDGES: only the cornice is arguably visible - there is a real shadow line at y=210 under a bright frieze band, with eaves overhang. Sills and a plat-band cordon over the ground floor are period-typical for this facade class and are the elements that matter above the 10 cm threshold. I set balconies false deliberately rather than inventing a balconet; nothing in the plate shows a projection and this house type often has none.

MATERIALS at 28 GHz: no plaster entry exists in the enum, so wall=concrete as the standard P.2040 proxy for render-on-masonry - plasterboard would be badly wrong here (eps ~2.9, an interior drywall value) for a solid rendered brick wall. trim=marble is the proxy for Belgian bluestone (Doornik), which is what the plinth, sills and surrounds will be on any Ghent house of this date. Roughness 0.8 mm: old painted lime render, slightly undulating and weathered, so a touch above the 0.5 mm smooth-render value but firmly in the material regime, not geometry. Brick bond and mortar joints are irrelevant here in any case - the facade is rendered.

SCENE CONTEXT for the generator, do not override with a generic street rule: fronting_street is Pensmarkt, highway=pedestrian, car_access=none. Place NO vehicles at this frontage. The correct clutter for Groentenmarkt is market stalls, cafe terrace furniture, bicycles against the plinth, bollards and the street trees - one of which is already occluding the right of the target in the plate and should be honoured in the twin, since it will shadow the ground-floor field. Detail budget belongs on the ground-floor openings and the cornice/eaves silhouette; the return elevation on Groentenmarkt (the 32.7 m footprint dimension) is not visible in set A and should inherit this grammar rather than receive independently invented detail.

reading.identification: Groot Vleeshuis, Ghent: a 1407-1419 late-Gothic brick market hall on the Groentenmarkt, one great single-volume hall under a very steep slate gabled roof with crow-stepped ends, now a public food hall.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE WARNING: both set B street photographs show a DIFFERENT building - a two-storey yellow-brick late-19th-c. structure with a slate mansard roof, pedimented dormer, segmental brick arches with alternating light headers, stainless ramp handrail and a "'t STAPEL huis" signboard, standing on block paving with parked cars. That is not the Groot Vleeshuis (wrong period, material, scale, massing, ground plane) and contradicts car_access=none on the gravel Vleeshuistragel. The photos are mis-geocoded to this OSM ID and were discarded in full; none of their features were carried into these parameters. Only plate A and knowledge of the building were used, hence the low-to-moderate confidence on facade-scale fields.

SEEN from plate A: the long continuous slate roof plane with its ridge running the length of the frontage, the overall low-wall/huge-roof massing, and the repeating rhythm of small pointed gables along the eaves. Nothing finer - the render dissolves well above mullion and reveal scale.

MASSING: building:levels=1 is correct and must be respected - this is one great hall, not a stacked building. Eaves at roughly 7.5 m, the remaining ~8.5 m of the confirmed 16 m is the steep roof (12.9 m depth at ~55 deg gives about that rise). Crow-stepped gables at both ends, ridge parallel to the Groentenmarkt frontage. The repeating gables along the long side are the 1542-43 "penshuizekes" - small houses built against the hall - plus their dormers; at ~4.9 m spacing over the 58.5 m frontage that gives 12 bays.

PHYSICS ALLOCATION: the >10 cm regime that matters is the deep window reveals in a roughly 0.6 m medieval wall, the stone sills and string courses, the corbelled eaves cornice, and the stepped gable copings - these are the facets and wedges that will govern street-level field on a corridor only 3.8 m away, and they should be explicit geometry. Hand-made brick with raked, weathered joints and the Balegem/Tournai stone banding stay as roughness (6 mm RMS) plus a scattering coefficient, never as mesh. Trim is set to "marble" as the nearest available dielectric proxy for the natural limestone dressings (eps ~7); "concrete" would be the fallback if the generator prefers it.

CLUTTER: no vehicles on either frontage. fronting_street is a gravel path with car_access=none, and the Groentenmarkt side is pedestrianised market surface. Populate with market stalls, bollards, bicycles, terrace furniture and bins instead - a parked-car rule applied here would be the same failure that filled the medieval square.

DETAIL BUDGET: spend it on the gable-end silhouettes, the eaves gable rhythm and the ground-floor portal, which is where the eye and the beam both go. The rear/river elevation deserves less.

reading.identification: The Graanspijker, a late-medieval/early-modern Ghent brick grain-staple warehouse on the Pensmarkt, turning a tall steep tiled gable to the narrow Vleeshuistragel alley beside the Groot Vleeshuis, three tall storage floors under a deep loft, heritage-listed and currently under restoration behind contractor hoarding.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE STATE: set B does not show this facade at all - the target is entirely behind white Denys site hoarding, scaffolding and a green temporary weather roof at the right frame edge. The crisp brick, sash joinery and stone plinth visible in set B belong to the buildings on the LEFT of the tragel and must not be attributed here. All facade fields are therefore inferred from building type; only massing and roof come from plate A.

HEIGHT LOGIC: 18 m confirmed over 3 levels only closes with warehouse storeys (4.5 / 4.0 / 4.0 -> ~12.5 m eaves, ~5.5 m gable). Across the 4.8 m alley frontage that is a very steep pitch, which is correct for a spijker - grain lofts are volume, not headroom - and matches the sharp apex in plate A. Do not substitute domestic 2.8 m storeys; they force a physically impossible roof.

GEOMETRY TO GENERATE (>10 cm, the regime that matters at 28 GHz): deep window reveals in thick brick, ~0.25 m, with segmental brick relieving arches and projecting Balegem limestone sills; a corbelled brick eaves table (muizentand) at the gable springing; stone gable coping with kneelers; a limestone plinth ~0.8 m at the base; iron wall anchors at floor levels. On the loft face, one hoisting door with a projecting timber hoist beam under the apex - this is the signature element of a graanspijker and is the strongest silhouette feature from any camera angle.

MATERIAL, NOT GEOMETRY: hand-formed small brick with recessed weathered lime joints is the 6 mm roughness figure plus a scattering coefficient. Do not mesh the bond. Trim is set to marble as the nearest EM proxy for Balegem/Tournai calcareous limestone dressings.

GROUND FLOOR: blank is deliberate. Vleeshuistragel is a gravel path, car_access=none, 1.1 m off the wall - a service flank, not a retail frontage. Place a single tall segmental-arched loading/service door within the blank plane; no shopfront, no glazing.

CLUTTER, and this is the one thing set B genuinely proves: the current state is a construction site. Place the white plank hoarding line, scaffolding standards, tarpaulin/temporary roofing and site signage along the alley face. Absolutely no parked vehicles - car access is none and the plate shows a pedestrian cobble/gravel tragel. Pedestrians and a parked bicycle at the Groentenmarkt end only.

DETAIL BUDGET: this wall is 1.1 m from the path, so it sits directly on the street-level corridor. Spend on reveals, the plinth, the arched door and the gable silhouette. The Pensmarkt flank and the party walls to the 5 attached neighbours are occluded and deserve almost nothing.

reading.identification: A small 16th–17th century brick 'penshuisje' (tripe-vendor's house) of the Pensmarkt row built against the flank of Ghent's Groot Vleeshuis — a 5 m-wide gable-fronted townhouse of two storeys plus attic under a crow-stepped gable, now in residential/small-commercial use.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE CAVEAT: the street photograph (set B) is misregistered — the magenta box outlines the timber palisade fence in the foreground of the opposite quay, and the target building does not appear in that frame. All fields that set B was expected to carry (wall material, window size and subdivision, sills, string courses, ground floor) are therefore inferred from building type, not observed. I have deliberately not read them off the Kraanlei/Graslei row visible across the water, which is a different street.

Set A (Google tiles) is melted but its silhouette is legible: the outlined unit reads as a narrow gable-fronted house with a jagged stepped crown, consistent with the unambiguously crow-stepped neighbours immediately to its left. That supports roof form and ridge orientation only. The lower half of the outlined box is occluded by foreground roof geometry, so the ground floor is unobserved.

HEIGHT: height_source is 'no-data', so 9.0 m is a default rather than a measurement. Split as ~5.9 m to eaves (3.0 + 2.9) with ~3.1 m of stepped gable above, the normal proportion for this house type. Storey count is inferred from that split, not counted in the image.

GEOMETRY THAT MATTERS AT 28 GHz: build the crow steps explicitly — 5–7 steps per rake, each a ~0.25 m tread with a stone coping, is the dominant scatterer for a receiver in the 0.9 m-wide Vleeshuistragel and will be sampled from every camera azimuth. Also mesh: the stone plinth/water table at the base, the sandstone speklagen string courses (~60–80 mm proud, keep only if they exceed 0.10 m; otherwise fold into roughness), window sills, and deep reveals in the massive masonry. Do NOT mesh brick bond, mortar joints or the sandstone/brick banding contrast — those live in the 1–10 cm regime and belong in roughness_mm and the scattering coefficient.

GROUND FLOOR: the fronting street here is the Vleeshuistragel, a gravel path with car_access=none, so this facade is the secondary alley elevation — a plain door and a single small window, no shopfront, no vehicles, no terrace. If the generator also builds the Pensmarkt elevation, that one plausibly carries a small café/shop glazing instead; do not mirror the alley treatment onto it.

CLUTTER: car_access=none on the fronting path is explicit — place no vehicles. Appropriate to the tragel: leaned bicycles, a wheelie bin, a downpipe, moss and rising damp on the lower 0.5 m of brick.

reading.identification: A surviving 'penshuisje' — one of the row of tiny tripe-sellers' shops built 1542-43 as a shallow 2.5 m lean-to against the north flank of Ghent's Groot Vleeshuis on Pensmarkt — two low storeys of weathered grey limestone rubble under small crow-stepped street-facing gables, ground floor a shop (latterly a frituur), currently shored and hoarded for restoration.
reading.notes:
Identification is anchored by the site's own interpretation panel (set B, image 1): the penshuisjes of 1542 beside the Groot Vleeshuis, the last surviving one now a frituur. Set A (3D tiles) is unusable — the whole range dissolves into untextured purple mush, so nothing below was read from it.

MASSING: do not extrude as a freestanding block. footprint_m 13.4 x 2.5 with area 32 m2 is a lean-to strip against the Vleeshuis flank; the rear wall is party wall (attached_neighbours 1) and the far taller Vleeshuis roof rises behind these small gables. An isolated 9 m box would read wrong from any rotated camera — this is exactly the visible-primitive failure.

ROOF: seen clearly in the enlarged crop — a repeating run of crow-stepped gable ends (trapgevels) with small stone pinnacles, each gable perpendicular to the street, hence ridge_parallel_to_street false. A green-slated pentice/penthouse roof slope runs below them; worth generating as geometry, it is a strong horizontal wedge at ~5-6 m and will matter for street-level scatter.

MATERIAL: wall is coursed grey limestone/sandstone rubble (Tournai bluestone with Balegem dressings), badly eroded, with brick patching and a whitewashed brick plinth at the near end. 'marble' is chosen as the closest available dielectric proxy for limestone (eps' ~7) — 'brick' (~3.75) and 'concrete' (~5.24) both understate it. roughness_mm 10 reflects genuinely rough rubble with deeply weathered raked joints; this is the 1-10 cm regime and must stay a roughness number, never meshed relief. trim 'wood' for the heavy timber ground-floor front, lintel beam and window joinery, which is what the beam actually meets at street level; note the window surrounds themselves are dressed stone.

GROUND FLOOR marked inferred, not seen: the front is boarded in dark timber and fenced off by white picket hoarding, so shopfront vs blank cannot be resolved from the image. 'shopfront' is the correct standing class given the documented frituur use and the wide timber front with a door opening under a beam.

STOREYS inferred: grade is hidden behind the hoarding so the count cannot be made from the image. 9.0 m is height_source 'no-data', so it is treated as ridge height, not eaves — 3.0 + 2.6 gives eaves ~5.6 m with the steep gable and crow-steps carrying the rest.

TEMPORARY WORKS: the bright yellow steel raking shores are restoration propping, not building geometry. Include them as scaffolding clutter if capture-time fidelity is wanted, but never as facades facets.

CLUTTER: fronting_street is highway=pedestrian with car_access=none — no parked vehicles anywhere on Pensmarkt. Correct clutter for this scene is the site hoarding and Denys signage, wheelie bins, a blue drum, pedestrians, and wet granite setts. Detail budget should go to the gable silhouettes, the crow-steps, the window reveals and the timber ground-floor front; the party-wall side deserves none.

reading.identification: Mid-C18 heritage-listed Ghent town house, narrow gable-end to Hooiaard square with its long 17 m flank forming the modelled facade on Schuddeveestraatje; red-painted brick with cream limestone blokbanden and a bluestone plinth, now in mixed residential/restaurant use.
reading.notes:
FACADE MODELLED = the long alley flank on Schuddeveestraatje (frontage_width 15.4 m of the 17 m footprint dimension); the 7 m gable end faces Hooiaard. Set A plate is degraded photogrammetry and supports nothing about this wall; all roof data is inferred from plot geometry and the row typology in B_1, where neighbouring Hooiaard houses show stepped and spout gables. The Hooiaard gable end is very likely stepped or spout-gabled — worth a separate grammar pass, it is the silhouette the square actually sees.

EVIDENCE SPLIT WITHIN BLOCKS (deliberate under-claiming): in `ledges`, the stone sills and the continuous cream sill-level band are genuinely visible in B_0, but the eaves cornice is above the crop, so the whole block is marked inferred rather than promote an unseen cornice. In `window`, width/height/glazing bars/grilles are seen; reveal_class is the weakest element — the left jamb of the near ground-floor window throws a real shadow, which is why I chose deep over shallow, but treat it as a judgement.

MATERIAL MAPPING: wall is hand-made brick, partly painted oxblood red, with irregular joints and patchy paint loss — roughness_mm 5 carries the 1–10 cm regime (brick relief, mortar joints, the blokbanden's shallow tooth pattern) and must NOT be meshed. Trim mapped to `marble` as the nearest available stone permittivity for the cream limestone dressings and the bluestone plinth; `concrete` would understate epsilon. The plinth is a distinct darker bluestone band ~0.9 m tall — worth its own material band if the generator supports one.

WHAT SHOULD BE EXPLICIT GEOMETRY (>10 cm): window reveals and the projecting stone surrounds, the continuous sill band, the corner quoin chain (the blokbanden project a few cm only — that is roughness, but the corner itself is a wedge and matters), the plinth offset, and the iron grilles over the ground-floor windows.

CLUTTER, CALIBRATED TO THIS ALLEY: car_access is `none` and the surface is sett — place NO vehicles here. B_0 shows the correct inventory: two grey metal utility cabinets standing against the plinth (~2.0 x 1.0 x 0.6 m, above the geometry threshold and strong scatterers at 1.1 m from the corridor), concrete planters with shrubs, a wheelie bin, leaning bicycles, galvanised soil pipes and ducting on the opposite wall, and the cafe terrace with rattan chairs and a maroon awning at the Hooiaard corner. The corner bay's ground floor is cafe glazing serving the restaurant; the alley elevation itself has no shopfront, which is why ground_floor is set to residential_door rather than shopfront.

HEIGHT BUDGET: 14.5 m adopted-photo read as ridge height. Ground 3.6 + two uppers at 3.0 gives eaves ~9.6 m, leaving ~4.9 m of roof — consistent with a steep Flemish pitch and an attic excluded from the storey count.

reading.identification: Wide, shallow brick corner town house of 1725 on the Hooiaard/Graslei junction in Ghent — a late-Baroque grain-quay house with low upper storage floors, listed locally (heritage 4) and now in restaurant use with a terrace on the pedestrian sett quay.
reading.notes: Set B's magenta box lands on the awning/terrace at the far left frame edge, so the target's facade is essentially not photographed; only the ground-floor use is legible there (café/restaurant, awning, bistro chairs, planters). The red-brick-with-cream-banding facade dominating set B is the NEIGHBOUR on Schuddevee and was deliberately not transcribed onto this building. Storey count and bay count come from set A's massing/rhythm, which is what those tiles carry; storey heights are apportioned arithmetic, not observation: 13.6 m to ridge minus a ~2.7 m roof rise (ridge-parallel gable over 5.9 m depth) leaves ~10.9 m of eave, which over four observed rows forces ~2.5 m uppers — low for a house but normal for a Graslei grain-quay building with storage lofts. Facade reads distinctly paler than the reddish neighbours in the same plate, hence painted/limewashed brick rather than exposed red brick; roughness 2.5 mm reflects paint over partly filled joints. Trim is Belgian bluestone (plinth, sills, window surrounds, band course) mapped to 'marble' as the closest dielectric proxy — 'concrete' would understate its permittivity. Roof marked inferred: the plate shows a broad plane above a straight eave, which supports ridge-parallel, but gabled-vs-half-hipped at the exposed Hooiaard end is not resolvable and one gable is a party wall to the single attached neighbour. CLUTTER: highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, sett surface — place NO vehicles on this frontage. Correct clutter, all visible in set B: projecting awning, rattan chairs and tables, chalkboard menu, grey planters, wall-mounted utility cabinet, bagged recycling, bikes. At 28 GHz the awning and terrace furniture are >10 cm geometry and likely matter more for street-level field than any facade ornament; brick bond and joint relief must stay in the roughness term, never meshed.

reading.identification: A four-storey plastered and white-painted Ghent corner commercial house on Hooiaard/Kortemunt, an older masonry core refronted in smooth lime render, with a modern dark-framed cafe/breakfast bar occupying the full ground floor and tall multi-light timber windows on the three floors above.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT WITHIN OBJECTS (schema forces one flag each, so stating it plainly):
- storeys: count=4 is genuinely seen (three window rows over a tall glazed ground floor, photo B0, and corroborated by building:levels=4). The 4.0/3.2 m split is NOT seen; it is apportioned inside the confirmed 16.0 m total, leaving ~2.4 m of gable/attic above the top ceiling. Treat the split as inferred.
- ledges: sills and the string course over the shopfront are seen in photo B1. The eaves cornice is inferred - the top of the building is cut off in every frame (both outlines dashed/clipped at the top). Absence of balconies is seen; the balconies visible in B1 belong to the buildings opposite, not to this one.
- bays: inferred. Both photographs are steeply oblique and photo B0's magenta box also contains further brick buildings behind the target, so counting window columns there is unsafe. 4 bays comes from 12.5 m frontage at ~3.1 m Ghent bay spacing, consistent with the ~1.35 m windows and ~1.8 m piers seen close up.
- roof: fully inferred. Not visible anywhere. Form from OSM. Ridge parallel to street because a 12.5 x 5.0 m footprint gives only a 2.5 m rafter run - a gable-to-street here would be an implausibly squat 12.5 m-wide gable, and this facade reads as a cornice-topped refront rather than a gable house. If a later oblique or aerial contradicts this, the ridge orientation is the first thing to overturn.

MATERIAL, and why it does not contradict the data: building:material=plaster describes the finish. I set the ray-tracing wall to ITU brick because a ~2 cm lime render over solid masonry is dielectrically brick-like (e' ~ 3.5-4.5), whereas ITU plasterboard is low-density gypsum board (e' ~ 2.94) and would materially under-predict reflection at 28 GHz. Photo B1 shows painted render with gentle undulation and no exposed joints, so roughness is 1.0 mm RMS, not the 3-8 mm of fair-faced brick - the render's function here is precisely to bury the 1-10 cm regime. Suggested scattering coefficient S ~ 0.2-0.3, near-specular. Trim=wood covers the heavy dark-painted timber upper joinery; the ground-floor frames may be metal-clad, which matters little as they are thin members against a large glass plane.

GEOMETRY WORTH MESHING (>10 cm, 1.07 cm wavelength):
- Shopfront piers between the cafe bays, roughly 0.4-0.5 m wide and standing ~0.10-0.15 m proud of the recessed glazing. These wedges are the main off-specular scatterers at pedestrian height and the ground floor is where the beam actually lands - spend budget here.
- The full-height ground-floor glass is a large flat specular plane; keep it flat, do not fake relief into it.
- Window sills, ~0.05-0.08 m projection, and shallow (~0.12 m) reveals on all upper openings.
- String course / fascia band over the shopfront, and the inferred eaves cornice.
- Projecting hardware seen in B0/B1: wall-mounted lamps, CCTV housings, a fire-service plate, window-box planters. Small but real silhouette breakers on an otherwise plain render plane.

SCENE CONTEXT: Hooiaard is highway=pedestrian with car_access=none. Place NO vehicles. The correct clutter, all seen: A-board menu chalkboards on the sett, folded and open parasols, timber planters with bamboo/box hedging, leaning bicycles, cafe tables. Ground is sett paving, which is itself a 3-8 cm relief regime - roughness, not geometry.

reading.identification: A 19th-century rendered and painted neoclassical/eclectic corner townhouse on the east side of Korenmarkt at the Kortemunt corner in Ghent, four storeys of flats over a pharmacy shopfront, under a slate pitched roof with the ridge parallel to the square.
reading.notes: Wall is painted cement/lime render over masonry, not fair-faced brick; 'concrete' is the closest dielectric proxy in the enum and roughness 0.6 mm keeps it in the material regime where it belongs (near-specular at 1.07 cm). Trim 'marble' stands for Belgian bluestone: the ground-floor plinth panels, door surround and (inferred) window sills. Only the plinth and surround are actually seen; sills, cornice and first-floor string course are supplied from the type, hence the ledges group is marked inferred even though a cornice band is faintly present in plate A. Roof read entirely from set A: a broad dark slate plane sloping to the square with the ridge across it. The useful finding is negative - there is no street-facing gable, so the Ghent stepped-gable prior must not fire on this building. Storey split 4.3 + 3 x 3.0 = 13.3 m to eaves, leaving 3.7 m of roof over an 8.5 m depth (~41 deg pitch), which closes on the measured 17.0 m without touching it. Detail budget: this facade is at 0 m from a pedestrian corridor, so spend it on the ground floor - the deep shopfront recess, the plinth, and the window reveals and cornice on the silhouette. CLUTTER: car_access none, highway pedestrian, paving_stones. No vehicles of any kind on this frontage. Set B shows the correct furniture - benches against the plinth, bike racks, cafe terrace, pedestrians - plus tram rails in the paving and catenary wire on poles overhead, both of which are real scatterers at this frequency and should not be dropped. Corner condition: two street frontages, so the Kortemunt return needs a facade too, not a blank party wall.

reading.identification: A tall four-storey brick town house of c. 1900 historicist Flemish-Renaissance type (a rebuild or heavy restoration on a medieval plot) at the Hooiaard corner beside the Groot Vleeshuis, with a crow-stepped gable, bluestone-banded facade and a commercial/café ground floor onto the pedestrian sett square.
reading.notes:
Sub-field evidence, stated explicitly so nothing gets promoted into the measured layer:

SEEN in set B at 5-6x magnification: brick wall colour and bond scale; crow-stepped gable with stone coping slabs on every step and red pantile roof behind; small lozenge opening in the gable field; continuous stone string courses at each floor plus a continuous stone sill band; stone jambs and segmental stone-and-brick arches around every opening; tall-narrow window proportion (roughly 1:2.2); absence of balconies on this facade.

INFERRED, not seen: reveal_class. Set B cannot resolve reveal depth; 'deep' is the prior for a ~40 cm solid brick wall with stone dressings, where the sash sits roughly 0.20 m behind the jamb face. If the generator wants a single number rather than a class, 0.20 m is my estimate, not a measurement. reading.identification: Late-19th/early-20th-century four-storey brick corner block at Pensmarkt/Hooiaard in Ghent's medieval core, retail at ground level with dwellings above, on an amalgamated 13.6 m frontage under a long street-parallel gabled roof with an inhabited attic.
reading.notes:

Everything on the wall is typological inference for this street and period.

BAY RHYTHM: measured, count inferred. Column-luminance autocorrelation over the upper-floor band (y 450-590) gives a single dominant peak at lag 58 px, r=0.70 — a real regular fenestration rhythm, not tile noise. Converting it to a count requires a horizontal scale I cannot pin down, because this is a corner building (street_frontages=2) and I cannot locate the return corner well enough to say how much of the ~420 px visible face is the 13.6 m Pensmarkt frontage versus the Hooiaard return. At ~25 px/m the 58 px period is ~2.3 m centres, giving 6 bays; that also sits mid-band for an amalgamated 13.6 m Ghent retail frontage. 5 bays at ~2.7 m centres is the live alternative — if the generator can tolerate it, 6 is the better default but this is the least-secure number in the set. Naive per-row minima detection returned 12-19 spurious peaks; ignore that, the autocorrelation is the trustworthy statistic.

HEIGHT BUDGET closes against the confirmed 16.0 m: 3.8 ground + 3 x 2.9 upper = 12.5 m eaves, leaving 3.5 m ridge rise over the 4.7 m half-span (footprint depth 9.4 m) for a ~37 deg pitch. That matches the moderate, non-steep slope in the plate. It also leaves a habitable attic, which is consistent with two pale rectangles resolvable on the front pitch — roof lights or small dormers. They are at the very edge of resolution and I cannot separate flush rooflight from dormer, so I have not claimed them; if the generator places roof openings on the front pitch, that is defensible, but do not mark them seen.

DO NOT INHERIT THE GRASLEI PRIOR. This is one block behind Graslei, and the reflex answer for that quarter is a stepped or spout gable turned end-on to the water. The plate contradicts it: eaves-to-street, ridge-along-street, unbroken across a 13.6 m plot. That plot width is itself the tell — it is two or three medieval plots merged, so the surviving-guild-house grammar (narrow, vertical, gable-fronted, deep stone reveals) is the wrong template here. I have set reveal_class to shallow (~0.12 m) accordingly: shallow is what a 19th-century brick wall with segmental arches gives. Deep reveals belong to thick medieval or stone walls and would put too much geometry into the facade.

TRIM MATERIAL: the real material is blue Belgian limestone (arduin), the Ghent default for sills, lintels and shopfront surrounds. The enum has no limestone, so I selected marble — both are calcium carbonate with eps' ~7 and similar loss, which is the correct dielectric behaviour at 28 GHz. Concrete would have been the wrong permittivity for the right-sounding reason. Please do not "correct" this to concrete downstream.

PHYSICS PARTITION. Above 10 cm, ask for explicit geometry: window reveals, the stone sills, the floor-level string courses, the eaves cornice, and the shopfront fascia and stallriser. Those wedges are what set street-level field in this narrow square. Between 1 and 10 cm — brick relief and recessed mortar joints — is the roughness_mm 4.0 figure and a diffuse scattering coefficient, never mesh. Ghent historic brick with raked joints sits at 3-5 mm RMS; I have taken 4.0. Below 1 cm is permittivity only.

CLUTTER CALIBRATION — read the tags. fronting_street is highway=pedestrian with car_access=none, distance 0.0 m. Place NO vehicles at this facade. Pensmarkt adjoins the Groentenmarkt and is a market and terrace square; the plate shows exactly that clutter class in the open paved area to the right of the building — market stalls or parasols, street trees, and people. That, plus terrace furniture, A-boards, bins and bike parking, is the correct population. A generic park-cars-along-every-street rule would fill this square wrongly.

DETAIL BUDGET. The building has two frontages, both public and both close to the corridor, so concentrate resolution on the ground-floor shopfront line and the window heads and sills of the first floor, and on the eaves and gable silhouette which is the only edge this plate actually verifies. The rear and the party walls carry attached neighbours on both sides and deserve almost nothing.

CONFIDENCE 0.5: macro layer is solid — height confirmed, levels, brick and gabled roof from OSM, roof orientation genuinely seen. The entire opening grammar is a defensible instance rather than a recovered truth, and no street photograph exists to close the gap.

BAY COUNT. 9.0 m frontage over 4 bays gives a 2.25 m module — 1.2 m opening on a 1.05 m pier, which is the rhythm A shows. Painted smooth render is genuinely smooth, hence 1.0 mm RMS; the banding grooves are shallow and sparse and do not justify pushing it toward a brick-like 3-8 mm. Wall is set to concrete as the standard proxy for render over masonry (the render is the surface the ray sees, not the brick behind it); trim is metal for the balustrade and shopfront framing, both directly visible.

CLUTTER — CHECK THE ACCESS TAG. fronting_street is pedestrian, surface sett, car_access none. Place NO vehicles on Hooiaard. The correct clutter, all of it visible in B, is cafe terrace furniture directly against this facade (timber tables, black metal chairs), folded parasols on masts, planters, bollards, and a tactile paving strip with embedded tram rails crossing the sett. This building is at distance_m 0.0 from the corridor, so it earns the full budget — concentrate it on the balcony assembly, the ground-floor glazing plane and its reveals, and the silhouette at the cornice. Do not spend equally on the return elevation or the roof slopes, which no plate resolves.

reading.identification: Late-19th-century rendered corner house at Korenmarkt/Kortemunt in Ghent, four storeys of flats over a pharmacy shopfront, distinguished by a painted timber canted oriel at first floor.
reading.notes:
STOREYS/ROOF ARE THE WEAK HALF. Set B's outline is dashed at the top, so no storey count is observable; the count is reconstructed from height_m 17.1 against a 5.3 m depth. 4.0 + 3x3.15 = 13.45 m eaves leaves 3.65 m of roof over a 5.3 m span, a ~54 deg Flemish pitch that lands on 17.1. Five storeys would leave ~1.1 m of roof, which this city does not build. A mansard is the plausible alternative to gabled for this period and would keep the same eaves line; if the generator supports it, mansard is roughly a coin-flip against gabled here. Ridge orientation follows the shallow plan (spanning the 5.3 m depth, parallel to Korenmarkt); as a corner unit with 2 street frontages it may carry a half-hip at the exposed end, which set A cannot resolve.

MATERIAL CHOICES. Wall is smooth painted cement render over masonry, not fair-face brick, so I chose concrete over brick: at 28 GHz the penetration depth is small enough that the render skin, not the brick substrate, sets the surface impedance. roughness_mm 0.6 is the smooth-render regime, deliberately far below the 3-8 mm you would give recessed brick joints. Trim = marble stands for the grey natural stone (Belgian blue stone) plinth and the smooth stone-look surrounds around the shopfront, which is the electrically distinct band at exactly the height a street-level beam hits. Caveat: the oriel itself is painted timber joinery, a different material from the trim value; if the generator can take a per-element override, the oriel box should be wood.

DETAIL BUDGET. distance_m 0.0 from the pedestrian corridor puts this building in the top tier. Spend it on the canted oriel: it must be real geometry, a three-sided corbelled projection roughly 2.6 m wide and 0.5-0.6 m deep spanning first floor, because it is the one feature that makes this facade a specific building rather than a rendered box, and at ~0.5 m projection it is firmly in the explicit-geometry regime. Second priority is the ground floor: the shop entrance is genuinely recessed (roughly 0.6-0.9 m behind the frontage line) and that reveal is a strong corner reflector at pedestrian height. Third, the string course and window sills as real ledges. Do NOT mesh the render texture or the moulding ornament - the panelled pilaster strips on the oriel and the fascia lettering are 1-5 cm relief and belong in the roughness/scattering coefficient, not the mesh.

CLUTTER. car_access is none on Korenmarkt and the photograph confirms it: trams and pedestrians only, no parked vehicles anywhere in frame. Do not place vehicles on this frontage under any rule. What the photo does show and what belongs here: bicycles parked loose against the facades, a bike trailer, freestanding timber terrace benches on the pavement directly in front of the neighbouring unit, and the tram rails set into the paving_stones. The projecting illuminated pharmacy cross is a real metre-scale metal object cantilevered off the wall at about first-floor level and is a legitimate scatterer if the generator has a signage class.

WHAT I DID NOT SEE. Bay count is inferred from 8.4 m frontage at a typical 2.7 m rhythm; the frame shows the oriel plus one adjacent opening and cuts off the rest. Window dimensions are read off the first-floor openings and assumed repeated up the elevation, which is standard for this type but not observed above the second floor.

reading.identification: A narrow 18th-19th century Ghent burgher house on Hooiaard, four storeys over a cafe/brasserie ground floor, eaves-to-street pitched roof, plastered or painted brick, terraced with party walls on both sides.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE. Only the roof is marked seen. Set A shows a broad slope above the target with a horizontal top edge running left-right and no street-facing gable peak, which supports eaves-to-street / ridge-parallel at this resolution. Form gabled rather than hipped follows from attached_neighbours=4 (party walls at both gable ends); the visibly hipped neighbour to the left is a different, freestanding-ended mass and should not be copied onto the target. Everything on the wall is inferred: the frontage spans only ~200 px of degraded photogrammetry, window slots are visible as blobs but bays cannot honestly be counted and a reveal class cannot be resolved.

HEIGHT CONSISTENCY. 4.0 ground + 3 x 3.0 upper = 13.0 m eaves; ~50 deg pitch over the 7.6 m depth adds ~4.5 m to the ridge = 17.5 m, matching the adopted-photo height. Do NOT re-derive storey heights from height_m independently or the roof volume gets absorbed into the wall and the eaves line lands too high. If the generator prefers a shallower pitch, take it out of the ridge, not out of the storeys.

CLUTTER - THE IMPORTANT ONE. fronting_street is pedestrian, sett, car_access=none, distance 0.0 m. NO parked or moving vehicles anywhere on Hooiaard. This is the exact case that previously filled a pedestrian square with individually-plausible cars. Correct clutter for this frontage: cafe terrace tables and chairs against the facade, parasols, A-boards, bike clusters, waste bins at the corners. Terrace furniture is 0.7-1.1 m tall scattering geometry directly in the street-level beam and is worth explicit facets; it matters more here than any facade ornament.

GROUND FLOOR. cafe_glazing chosen over generic shopfront because Hooiaard at the head of the Graslei is a brasserie strip, not a retail run. Expect a large glazed opening nearly filling the bay width with a recessed entrance door, a fascia/signage band above, and the glass plane set back 0.3-0.5 m from the upper-storey wall plane. That setback is a real wedge at 28 GHz and should be geometry, not texture.

PHYSICS SPLIT. Explicit geometry (>10 cm): window reveals at the shallow class (~0.12 m), stone sills, the plat band string course between ground and first floor, the eaves cornice with its overhang, the ground-floor glazing setback, chimney stacks on the ridge. NOT geometry (1-10 cm): brick coursing, mortar joints, painted-render texture, any moulding profile detail. Those are carried entirely by roughness_mm = 3.0. If the facade is stucco rather than painted brick, drop roughness to ~0.5; 3.0 is a deliberate hedge between the two, since the uniform pink in the plate is equally consistent with red brick and with painted render and set A cannot separate them.

TRIM. marble is used as the natural-stone dielectric proxy for Belgian blue limestone (arduin), which is the near-universal sill, plinth and surround material in Ghent. Expect a stone plinth 0.4-0.8 m at pavement level. If the generator has a distinct limestone entry, prefer it over marble.

VERTICAL RHYTHM. Windows should diminish upward in the Flemish manner: first floor at the stated 2.1 m, second ~1.9 m, third ~1.6 m, widths held constant at 1.2 m so the bay centrelines stay aligned. Uniform window heights on all four storeys is the tell of a generic template. Glazing bars true: a T-division or small-pane pattern, but render this as material and fine relief, never as meshed muntins at 28 GHz.

DETAIL BUDGET. distance_m = 0.0 on a pedestrian street means this facade is at eye level and in the beam; spend on the ground floor, the openings and the silhouette edges (cornice, ridge, chimneys). street_frontages = 2 with an 18.7 m depth implies a rear elevation, plausibly toward the Leie quay: give it the same grammar at reduced budget, plainer, fewer ledges, no cafe glazing.

CONFIDENCE. 0.5 reflects a solid roof reading, a height-corroborated storey count, and a bay count plus full wall grammar that rest on Ghent building stock rather than on this image.

The return elevation should carry the same render, sill and cornice grammar but with a sparser and more irregular bay rhythm, and a largely blank or service-doored ground floor rather than a second shopfront.
