reading.identification: A 16th–17th-century Flemish brick-and-stone quay house on the Korenlei in Ghent, heritage-listed, four storeys on a narrow 9.1 m gable-fronted plot with stone cross-mullioned windows and a scroll-consoled gable, in mixed residential/hospitality use on the pedestrianised Leie waterfront.
reading.notes:
Read almost entirely from set B photo 0, which is the target's own quay elevation at close range and steep oblique; photo 1's box is loose and brackets the stuccoed classicist neighbour and the KorenleiTwee terrace as well, so I took no material or ground-floor evidence from it. Plate A is unusable for this building — the tile mesh shreds the gable into spikes and the facade into a purple smear.

STOREYS/BAYS: four window rows countable above the quay plus the gable stage. 3.8 + 3x3.2 = 13.4 m to the eaves, leaving ~3.3 m of gable/attic to reach the measured 16.7 m — consistent. Three window axes at roughly 3 m centres across the 9.1 m frontage; the extreme obliquity means a fourth axis cannot be ruled out, but three is what the photo supports. Note the 9.1 x 5.3 m footprint is the front range only; the real plot runs much deeper behind, so do not read the 5.3 m as building depth for the roof solid.

WINDOWS: stone kruisvensters — central mullion, transom in the upper third, leaded small-pane glazing in the upper lights, red-painted timber frames below. Glazing bars are directly resolved. Reveal read as deep: the stone surrounds sit in a ~0.4 m brick wall and throw real shadow on the jambs at this grazing angle.

GEOMETRY vs MATERIAL (28 GHz): put as explicit facets — the stone window surrounds and their reveals, the continuous stone sill and lintel courses that band the brick horizontally across the whole frontage, the brick segmental relieving arches above the openings (clearly proud of the wall plane), the two wrought-iron balconettes (one at the gable window, one at second floor), and the gable's volute scroll consoles. All exceed 10 cm relief and are what will scatter off-specular into the quay canyon. Keep as roughness only — the hand-moulded brick bond and its deeply eroded recessed joints; 7 mm RMS is high for brick stock and is justified here by visible weathering and washed-out mortar. Do not mesh it.

TRIM: 'marble' is standing in for Belgian bluestone / Balegem sandstone dressings, chosen as the closest dense-limestone dielectric in the enumeration; if the generator has a limestone entry, prefer it. Timber frames are a sub-facet detail, not the trim class.

ROOF: inferred, and flagged as such. The box runs off the top of frame 0, so the gable profile is cut. What I can see is a pair of large stone volute scrolls flanking a narrow upper stage with a balconied window, and a slate plane receding away from the water — that reads as a bell/neck gable, ridge perpendicular to the quay, and rules out crow-steps (a stepped silhouette would be unmistakable). If the generator supports a neck gable (halsgevel) distinct from a bell gable, that is the better fit. Roof covering is slate, not tile.

GROUND FLOOR: inferred. The lowest window row is the same cross-window type as above, with no shopfront, fascia or display glazing on this elevation; the brick arch at the very bottom of frame 0 is the quay retaining wall below street level, not the building. Residential door is the defensible instance for a heritage house here, but hospitality use is common on this row and cafe_glazing would be the alternative if a plot-level POI says so.

CLUTTER: fronting_street is pedestrian, sett, car_access none. No parked or moving vehicles on this frontage at any distance — this is exactly the case where a generic parked-car rule would fill the Korenlei with a hundred illegal vehicles. Correct dressing is terrace tables and chairs, parasols, bollards and chain rails along the quay edge, bins, leaning bicycles, planters and A-boards, plus pedestrians. Photo 1 confirms all of these on the quay. The sett paving is itself a >1 cm relief surface but well under 10 cm — treat as ground roughness, not geometry.

reading.identification: A heritage-listed 17th-century Flemish traditional-style brick-and-sandstone corner house at Hooiaard / Schuddeveestraatje in Ghent's old harbour quarter, red-painted brick with cream sandstone quoins and window surrounds over a bluestone plinth, now in restaurant use with a glazed, awninged ground floor and pavement terrace.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT. Seen in set B: painted brick wall with spalled paint over irregular handmade brick; cream-painted sandstone toothed quoins at the corner and around openings; bluestone plinth ~0.8 m; projecting stone sills; tall multi-light windows with iron bars (diefijzers) and clearly recessed glazing planes; café glazing under a retractable awning, chalkboard, festoon lights, bistro terrace. Seen in set A (only roof view, photogrammetry heavily smeared): one pitched plane, ridge along the long axis of the block, eaves line legible, no dormer resolvable.

STOREYS marked inferred: the magenta outline in set B runs off the top of the frame, so the building continues above the photo. Two upper storeys plus the shopfront are directly visible; count=3 with 3.5 m ground and 3.1 m upper reconciles that against the 13.6 m adopted height, leaving ~3.9 m of roof over a 4.8 m depth (~58 deg pitch, steep but normal for this quarter). If the generator prefers a shallower roof, 4 storeys at ~2.85 m is the alternative reading; I did not see enough to choose.

BAYS marked inferred: the corner is ambiguous as to which face carries the 13.9 m frontage. I count four large openings on the long face; 13.9/4 = ~3.5 m bay pitch, which fits either reading of the corner.

LEDGES marked inferred as a group because the cornice is not seen — the wall is cut off in set B and set A resolves only a bright eaves band. Sills, the horizontal stone band above the shopfront, and the absence of balconies are directly seen; a modest corbelled brick eaves is the prior for this type.

PHYSICS. The sandstone toothing that makes this facade legible projects only 2-4 cm and the brick relief 3-8 mm. Both sit in the 1-10 cm regime: do NOT mesh the toothing, the speklagen or the joints. They are carried by roughness_mm = 6 (plain historic brick ~4 mm, raised for the localised 2-4 cm stone toothing). Only the window reveals, the projecting sills, the plinth nosing and the eaves exceed 10 cm and deserve explicit geometry. trim = marble is the closest dielectric proxy in the enum for Belgian bluestone (dense limestone, eps ~7) and the Balegem sandstone dressings; concrete would under-state permittivity for the plinth, which is the trim element the beam actually sees at street level.

CLUTTER. fronting_street has car_access=none on sett-paved living_street. No parked vehicles on Schuddeveestraatje. Correct clutter for this frontage: bistro chairs and tables with cushions, zinc planters with rosemary/laurel, two utility cabinets against the plinth, wall-mounted stainless extract ducting on the alley side, wheelie bins, refuse sacks, and bicycles.

DETAIL BUDGET. The building is 0.9 m from the corridor, so it earns full treatment on openings and the ground floor; the roof is the weakest-evidence element and should not be over-articulated.

reading.identification: Early-18th-century (1714) Ghent narrow-plot burgher/merchant house on the Hooiaard wharf by the Leie, listed heritage, presenting a 6.4 m three-bay gable front to the Schuddeveestraatje alley over a deep 18 m plot, with a commercial ground floor under four upper storeys and an attic in the street gable.
reading.notes:
Plate is heavily degraded for this target: clipped at frame top (no roof visible) and the lower ~55% is occluded by a smeared foreground mass (bridge parapet / quay blob). Only ~2.5 window rows of upper facade are legible. Bay count (3 columns) is the sole field the imagery genuinely supports.

Height budget drives the storey call: 3.8 + 3x3.0 = 12.8 m eaves, leaving ~4.1 m of gable to reach the measured 16.9 m — the signature of a gable-front house, not a cornice building. Five storeys would leave only ~1.5 m above the top floor and is rejected on that basis. Measured window pitch in-plate (~135 px, naive scale ~3.0 m) is consistent.

Softest field is roof form. 1714 is Ghent's late-Baroque window, so klokgevel (bell_gable) is the prior; spout_gable (tuitgevel) is the plausible alternative and a defensible swap. Stepped gable is explicitly rejected as 16th-century vocabulary — two centuries early for this start_date, and it is the generic-Flemish template worth resisting here.

Wall is painted render over brick: roughness 1.5 mm sits in the 1-10 cm scattering regime, not geometry — do not mesh bond or joints. Neighbouring facades in-plate read pinker/redder (exposed brick); this target reads paler grey-lilac, hence render, though at 25 cm/texel that is a weak cue and the field stays inferred. Trim = concrete as the ITU proxy for sandstone dressings (sills, waterlijsten, gable coping).

Ledges are all >10 cm and belong as explicit geometry: sandstone sills ~15-20 cm proud, moulded floor-level band courses, cornice under the gable. Balconies false — no projecting elements on the target in-plate, and an alley this narrow would not carry them.

CLUTTER CONSTRAINT, read before populating the street: fronting_street car_access = none, surface sett, living_street, 1.0 m offset. Place zero vehicles on Schuddeveestraatje. The alley is also too narrow for a cafe terrace, which is why ground_floor is shopfront rather than cafe_glazing — a glazed ground plane with a recessed entrance, no terrace furniture. Bikes and bins against the wall are appropriate; parked cars are not.

Detail budget: the building sits 1.0 m off the corridor, so it earns full resolution on openings, sills and the ground-floor glazing. Spend it on the gable silhouette and the window reveals, which is where the off-specular return at 28 GHz is decided.

reading.identification: A 19th-century heritage-listed corner house on Hooiaard at the mouth of Schuddeveestraatje in Ghent's old port quarter, built or re-fronted in the neo-traditional Flemish manner: red-painted brick with white-painted stone toothed quoins and cross-mullioned windows over a bluestone plinth, four storeys, with a cafe occupying the ground floor and a terrace under a retractable awning.
reading.notes:
Evidence weighting: B_0 is close-range (~1 m) and carries essentially all the reliable detail — wall material, quoining, window subdivision, sills, plinth, ground-floor use. Plate A is tile-mesh smear at this range and supports massing only. B_1's magenta box straddles two unrelated facades (a white bay-windowed one and a green-painted one) at long range through a fisheye and matches neither the brick nor the quoins in B_0; I treated it as low-information rather than as contradicting B_0, which is the main reason confidence is 0.55 rather than 0.75.

Frontage orientation is the load-bearing uncertainty. footprint 15.4 x 5.2 with frontage_width 14.6 is ambiguous about which side faces which street. The 2D box in B_0 compresses the receding wall to a narrow x-range, which reads as the 5.2 m end facing Schuddeveestraatje and the 14.6 m frontage running away along Hooiaard; addr:street=Hooiaard agrees. Bay count is therefore set for the Hooiaard face and marked inferred. If the generator instead places 14.6 m along the alley, re-derive bays at ~2.9 m spacing and expect barred windows over the plinth there rather than glazing.

Storey stack is a reconciliation, not an observation: 15.4 m to ridge, less ~2.6 m for a 45-degree roof over a 5.2 m span, leaves ~12.8 m of wall, i.e. 3.8 + 3 x 3.0. B_0 is cut off at the top of frame so the full stack was never visible.

Geometry vs roughness. Explicit facets (>10 cm regime): the toothed quoin strips up the corner and returning around every opening, the projecting stone window surrounds and sills, the bluestone plinth offset, the awning box. These are the scattering features that matter for a wall standing 1.2 m off the corridor, and they are exactly what a plain extruded footprint would lose. NOT geometry (1-10 cm regime): brick relief, mortar joints, the patches where red paint has spalled to bare brick — these are the 4 mm RMS number. The wrought-iron window bars (~2 cm rod at ~10 cm pitch) sit on the boundary and are better omitted than meshed coarsely.

Trim is set to marble as the dielectric proxy for the bluestone plinth and the painted limestone/sandstone surrounds; there is no dense-limestone entry in the enum. Wall roughness is raised slightly above smooth-render values because repeated overpainting has partly filled joints while paint loss has opened others.

Clutter, calibrated to this street and not to Europe generally: car_access is none on a sett-surfaced living_street, so place no vehicles on Schuddeveestraatje. Correct clutter, all of it visible in B_0: cafe terrace tables, stacked rattan chairs and cushions plus lead-grey planters at the Hooiaard end under the awning; two grey utility cabinets and a ground-level planter against the alley wall; wall-mounted galvanised vent ducting and downpipes; wheelie bins and a leaning bicycle further down the alley; overhead cabling across the alley.

Detail budget: spend it on the corner pier and the first two bays either side of it, the ground floor, and the alley elevation. The rear long wall and anything above the eaves deserve much less.

reading.identification: A late-16th/17th-century Ghent patrician canal house on the Korenlei quay in traditional Flemish brick-and-sandstone style, four storeys of hand-made brick with sandstone cross-windows under a steep slate roof crowned by a scrolled bell-profiled gable, heritage-listed and in hospitality use at quay level.
reading.notes:
Wall, windows and ledges read from set B photo 1, where the outline is tight on a brick facade seen obliquely from the quay (Groot Vleeshuis and Gravensteen behind confirm the camera looks north along Korenlei). Clearly resolved there: sandstone kruiskozijnen (mullion + transom, four lights), leaded small-pane upper lights, red-painted timber frames, deep chamfered stone reveals, continuous sandstone sill bands running across the wall as string courses, segmental brick relieving arches, red-painted timber eaves cornice, a wrought-iron balconet at the gable window plus a second dark balustrade one floor down, and stone volute scrolls flanking the crowning gable.

Set B photo 0 conflicts: its box lands on a white-rendered Baroque facade with a rococo corner niche, black awning and restaurant terrace, materially incompatible with the brick of photo 1. Either it is the parcel's second frontage (street_frontages: 2) or the projection slipped onto a neighbour. I used it only as weak support for hospitality use at ground level, hence ground_floor is marked inferred, not seen. The target's own quay-level storey is below the frame bottom in photo 1.

Storeys: three window rows are directly visible and the ground floor is cut off; count 4 is the reconciliation of those rows with the 17.1 m height datum (3.8 + 3x3.3 = 13.7 m to eaves, leaving ~3.4 m of gable). Per-storey heights are priors, so the whole block is inferred.

Set A is badly degraded photogrammetry but supports two things: the roof is dark slate rather than the red pantile of the eastern neighbours, and a raised vertical element faces the quay. Gable form (bell_gable, standing for a Flemish scrolled neck/klokgevel, which the enum has no exact term for) and the ridge-perpendicular-to-street orientation come from photo 1, where the slate-clad ogee raking edge and its stone volutes are visible against the sky.

Material mapping: the dressings are Balegem sandstone. Emitted as concrete (ITU eps_r ~5.24) rather than marble (7.07) because the concrete dielectric is the closer proxy for sandstone; the label reads wrong, the physics reads right. Roughness 6 mm covers hand-made brick with eroded and raked lime joints, weathering streaks and the flat brick relieving arches - all of which sit in the 1-10 cm band and must stay a roughness number, not geometry.

Detail budget: put the explicit geometry on the deep window reveals, the projecting sill and cordon bands, the two balconets, the eaves cornice and the gable volutes. All are above 10 cm and all sit on the silhouette or around the openings.

Street context, do not violate: fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access none on sett paving, so no parked or moving vehicles anywhere on this frontage. The clutter that belongs is terrace tables and chairs, planters, umbrellas, A-boards, bollards, hanging restaurant banners (KorenleiTwee signage is visible on this stretch), quay railings, moored tour boats and a quay-wall segmental arch at water level.

reading.identification: Mid-18th-century (Louis XV/rococo) Ghent canal-front townhouse on Korenlei: a narrow three-bay dressed-sandstone burgher house with carved rocaille window surrounds, balustraded aprons and a slate mansard with a curved bell-dormer, heritage-listed, now retail/restaurant at ground level with dwellings above.
reading.notes:
GEOMETRY BUDGET (>10 cm, worth meshing): (1) the mansard — a two-slope roof with the lower slope at ~70 deg, terminated by a projecting moulded eaves cornice ~0.35 m deep; (2) three street dormers on that lower slope, the central one a voluted bell-dormer with a round-arched head and scrolled flanks, the two flankers smaller with segmental heads (plate A resolves all three; sv1 shows the centre one in detail); (3) window reveals ~0.22 m within moulded architraves; (4) continuous stone sills and inter-storey string/panel bands; (5) balustraded aprons under the first-floor windows — short runs of turned stone balusters projecting ~0.15 m, clearly resolved in street photo _0; (6) the ground-floor awnings, which are large fabric planes cantilevered ~1.8 m over the quay and are strong specular blockers at 28 GHz — model them, they matter more than any brick relief.

NOT GEOMETRY (1-10 cm): ashlar joints, the carved rocaille cartouches and keystones, tooling on the stone. These go into roughness_mm = 2.5 and a scattering coefficient. Meshing the carving would produce specular garbage.

MATERIAL CAVEAT: the wall is natural calcareous sandstone ashlar (Lede/Balegem), not brick and not render — street photo _0 resolves individual block joints and monolithic carved elements. The enum has no stone class, so `marble` is used as the dielectric proxy (eps_r ~7, right for limestone/sandstone; `concrete` at 5.2 would be too low). Visually it must read as warm weathered cream-grey ashlar with soiling streaks, NOT polished marble. roughness_mm = 2.5 is an inferred derived value for fine-tooled ashlar with thin recessed lime joints; no image resolves RMS height. Everything else in the material block (wall identity, dark-painted timber joinery) is photographed.

STREET CONTEXT — read the data, do not apply the parked-car prior: fronting_street is Korenlei, highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, surface=sett. ZERO vehicles. Populate instead with what both street photos actually show against this frontage: café terrace furniture (rattan chairs with sheepskin throws, small tables), large black square parasols on heavy bases, stainless bollard-and-rope terrace edging, patio heaters, A-board menu signs, a large planted tub, parked bicycles in clusters, and pedestrians. Paving is granite sett, wet-toned.

CORNER CONDITION: street_frontages = 2 and attached_neighbours = 2 — this is a corner unit on a narrow footprint (10.2 x 8.3 m). Apply the same bay rhythm, sill/cornice grammar and ashlar to the return elevation; street photo _0 shows the return carrying a glazed shopfront with stallriser and transom under its own awning. The party walls to left and right are blind.

DETAIL GRADIENT: the building sits 3.5 m from the pedestrian corridor, so it earns full budget on the ground floor, the openings and the silhouette (cornice, dormers, gable scrolls). The rear and roof planes away from the quay can drop to plain planes.

WEAK EVIDENCE FLAGS: window width/height are scaled from the 7.3 m frontage divided across 3 bays, cross-checked against the pane grid in photo _0 — good to about +/-0.15 m. The mansard is confirmed by plate A massing and the slate slope in sv1, but its rear pitch and any rear dormers are unobserved. Ground-floor storey height is inferred from the awning line and shopfront proportions since the base is partly occluded in every view.

flags: roof form marked `seen`, but no view here looks down on it

reading.identification: A narrow single-unit slice of a 16th–17th century brick-and-sandstone merchant quay house on Korenlei, Ghent, three storeys plus attic over a river-level cellar, 5.4 m frontage carrying 15.1 m of height, now in mixed residential/horeca use on a protected canal-front row.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE BASE. Both street photos (set B) are shot from the water, i.e. they show the REAR/canal elevation, not the Korenlei front. Set A is photogrammetry that has melted into unusable shards precisely inside the target box — I read nothing from it and recommend no one else does either.

STOREYS — marked inferred, but split: the COUNT of 3 is seen (three window rows above quay level in both photos). The metre values are inferred, apportioned against the measured 15.1 m: 4.0 + 3.2 + 3.2 = 10.4 m, leaving ~4.7 m of gable/roof, which is consistent with the steep pitch this typology carries. Because two of the three numbers in this group are inferred, the group is marked inferred rather than promote a guess into the measured layer.

CELLAR STOREY — important and not captured by the schema. Photo 1 shows the masonry continuing BELOW the Korenlei pavement datum down to the waterline, with a small punched opening at cellar level and then a plain quay wall to the water. The count of 3 excludes this, per "storeys above ground." For the ray tracer, do not terminate the facade at the street datum on the canal side: there is roughly 3-4 m of additional wetted quay wall acting as a large, near-flat reflector, and a grazing-incidence water surface below that. On this corridor that geometry likely matters more than anything on the upper facade.

BAYS — inferred, not seen. Both views are oblique or partial; photo 0 shows what may be two windows per floor but plausibly straddles two different wall planes (front bay vs recessed section), and photo 1's box covers a strip narrower than the full frontage showing one window per floor. 2 is the prior for 5.4 m: 2 x 1.4 m openings with stone piers between and at the jambs. Treat as a candidate, not a measurement.

ROOF — inferred, low confidence, and the weakest field here. Gabled with ridge perpendicular to the quay is the canonical Graslei/Korenlei form for a deep narrow plot (6.3 x 3.7 m), and I am applying it as a prior. The raking brick gable end with hoist opening visible in photo 1 belongs to the NEIGHBOUR, not the target, so it is corroboration of the row typology only. Note also that the enum conflates structure with dressing: the roof is structurally a perpendicular gable, but the quay-front gable is very likely dressed as a stepped (trapgevel), spout (tuitgevel) or voluted neck gable (halsgevel) — a voluted example with stone scrolls is clearly visible on the adjacent house in photo 0. If the generator supports gable dressing as a separate knob, set it; stepped and bell are both defensible instances for this row. A flat top would be badly wrong and is the classic "visible primitive" failure.

GROUND FLOOR — inferred, zero direct evidence. Chose residential_door over cafe_glazing deliberately despite the restaurant context. This is a protected facade; its ground floor is masonry with punched stone-framed openings (tall stone-framed door plus stone-framed windows), NOT a modern glazed shopfront. The radio consequence is the point: punched masonry scatters, a continuous glass plane specularly reflects. If ground-truth later shows horeca occupancy behind, that does not change the opening geometry.

MATERIAL / PHYSICS REGIME SPLIT.
- >10 cm, give these explicit geometry: window reveals (~0.20-0.25 m, stone cross-window frames with the leaded lights set back behind the mullion and transom); projecting stone sills; the continuous stone string courses running the full frontage at sill and lintel level; the eaves cornice with its timber fascia; brick relieving arches over openings. On a frontage only 5.4 m wide the string courses are the dominant off-specular feature — they are horizontal, continuous and unbroken across the whole facade, so they will drive street-level and over-water field far more than the window count does.
- 1-10 cm, roughness ONLY, do not mesh: the brickwork. Hand-made irregular Flemish brick, weathered, with deeply eroded lime mortar joints and noticeable coursing unevenness. 6 mm RMS. Suggest a scattering coefficient around S = 0.3-0.4, at the high end for masonry, because this is genuinely eroded rather than sharp modern brick. Meshing this relief would produce specular garbage, not extra realism.
- <1 cm, material only: brick permittivity for the wall field. Trim is set to concrete as a DIELECTRIC PROXY for Balegem sandstone (ITU concrete eps' ~5.24 sits close to calcareous sandstone; marble at ~7.07 is too high and would also render as polished white, which is visually wrong). The trim is pale grey-buff dressed stone, not concrete, in appearance. Window frames are dark-stained and red-painted timber, a secondary trim not representable in a single enum slot.

BALCONIES — false for this unit. Photo 0 does show two small wrought-iron balconies and photo 1 shows a metal terrace platform, but all of them fall on adjacent units outside the target box. Do not let the neighbour's ironwork bleed onto this frontage.

GLAZING — glazing_bars true is firmly seen: leaded small-pane glazing is resolved in photo 0. Note these are true divided lights, so the glazed area is subdivided at roughly 20-30 cm pitch. That is right at the boundary of the geometry regime; treat the bars as material/roughness on the glass panel rather than as modelled mullions, but DO model the stone mullion and transom themselves, which are ~15-20 cm and structural.

CLUTTER — the fronting street is pedestrian, sett-surfaced, car_access none. Place NO vehicles on Korenlei. This is exactly the failure mode that filled a medieval square with parked cars. What the photos actually show and what belongs here: café terrace furniture and white parasols, planters and small trees, hanging vertical banners on brackets projecting from the facade, string lighting, wheelie bins, moored boats and a floating pontoon against the quay wall, and heavy metal downpipes running the full height of the facade (clearly visible and worth including — a vertical metal cylinder against masonry is a real scatterer). Detail budget should concentrate on the water-facing elevation and the quay wall, since that is what the corridor illuminates; the Korenlei front is unobserved and should get the typology default, not invented specificity.

reading.identification: A tiny modern timber service structure — OSM building=roof, 4.4 × 1.9 m, 8 m² — an open-sided lean-to canopy and enclosure standing on the gravel Vleeshuistragel towpath against the river flank of Ghent's 15th-century Groot Vleeshuis, its path-side face closed by a white-painted pointed-top timber palisade with dark-stained timber posts behind.
reading.notes:
WHAT THIS IS NOT: do not apply a Ghent canal-house grammar here. The magenta box in set A lands on the Groot Vleeshuis flank (tall two-light arch-headed openings in brick/sandstone) purely because Google tiles contain no geometry for an 8 m² canopy — that wall is the NEIGHBOUR, behind the target. Set A's left third is this same white palisade, photogrammetrically melted into a spiky crest; that is the only part of A that touches the target at all. Read nothing about storeys, fenestration or material off A.

HEIGHT: height_source is "no-data", so 9.0 m is a fallback, not a measurement, and I am not treating it as macro truth. The visible fabric is a ~2.8–3.0 m palisade with dark timber rising a little above it; total mass reads ~4 m to the eaves. I have set one storey at 4.0 m. If the pipeline is hard-bound to 9.0 m, the surplus belongs to the Vleeshuis wall this thing leans on, not to this prism — a 9 m tall 4.4 × 1.9 m timber slab on a towpath would be a visible-primitive failure from any rotated camera.

BAYS / OPENINGS: bays=1 is a formality — the towpath face is continuous boarding with no window column anywhere across the 4.1 m frontage, seen at 1–3 m in B. Preferred generation is ZERO openings. The window block is a floor value only; if the grammar insists on punching one, make it a flush unglazed gap in the boarding, never a framed sash.

CORNICE, read correctly: true here means a timber eaves fascia with roughly 0.2–0.3 m of overhang shading the path — the serrated dark-brown edge above the palisade top-right in B. It is emphatically NOT a moulded masonry cornice. That overhang is the single most valuable >10 cm feature on this object: it is the wedge that produces the near-field diffraction at 3.1 m from the path centreline. Model the fascia and the eaves line as geometry; model the roof pitch falling from the Vleeshuis party wall toward the water.

PALISADE — the physics point that matters most: the boards are separated by open gaps of roughly 15–20 mm, i.e. 1.5–2 λ at 28 GHz. This screen is partially TRANSMISSIVE, not a solid wall. Treating the towpath face as a closed dielectric slab will overstate blockage and kill the field that actually leaks through onto the path. If the generator supports it, model the palisade as a slatted plane with real gaps (board pitch ~120 mm, board width ~100 mm, thickness ~22 mm) rather than as a filled facade; if it cannot, at minimum apply a transmission/porosity term of order 0.15.

MATERIAL: painted sawn softwood, near-white and chalky with grey weathering streaks and rust-stained nail holes. 2.5 mm RMS covers the board cupping and the chamfered arrises — the board-to-board steps and the gaps are handled as the slat geometry above, not folded into roughness twice. Trim (posts, rails, the return screen) is dark-stained near-black timber, distinctly lower albedo than the palisade; that contrast is the main visual read from the path and should not be flattened to one wood shader.

CLUTTER: fronting_street is a gravel path with car_access=none. Place no vehicles, no parking, no kerb. Correct ground clutter for a Ghent towpath is gravel with weed tufts at the fence line (both visible in B), the steel pipe railing on the water side, and possibly a moored boat. Ground material under and around this structure is loose gravel, not paving.

flags: storeys fill only 44% of the envelope

reading.identification: A narrow gable-fronted brick-and-sandstone burgher/quay house on the Graslei, 17th-century in origin and restored or partly rebuilt for the 1913 Ghent World's Fair, standing on a deep 22 m plot running back from the Leie with its short gable end to the water and a café-occupied ground floor at quay level.
reading.notes:
READ FROM PLATE: the lower band of facade in set A is the Leie reflection / tile LOD duplication, not a second storey group — only the upper band was used. The magenta box is a footprint bounding box, ~2x the 8.6 m frontage in screen width, so it straddles both neighbours; bay count was NOT taken from it.

STOREYS: derived from height_m 11.6 (data), not counted. A gable-fronted Graslei house of this modest size carries three full storeys to the gable springing (3.6 + 2.8 + 2.8 = 9.2 m) with the attic inside the ~2.4 m gable. The apparent fourth window row in the plate is the attic light in the gable, which is why count excludes it.

ROOF: stepped gable (trapgevel) is the Graslei row idiom and the immediate right-hand neighbour in the plate shows one clearly, with finials — but I could not attribute a specific gable profile to the target at this resolution, hence inferred. Ridge perpendicular to the quay follows directly from 8.6 m frontage on a 9.7 x 22.3 m footprint.

TRIM MATERIAL: "concrete" is a dielectric proxy for Balegem/Ledian sandstone dressings (bandeaux, window surrounds, gable copings), whose dry permittivity sits near ITU concrete rather than marble. Do NOT render it as concrete — it is pale honey-grey ashlar banding against dark red-brown brick. That brick/stone alternation is the strongest visual signature of this row and must be albedo plus the string-course geometry, never a painted stripe.

28 GHz BUDGET: put geometry into (a) the horizontal sandstone string courses between storeys, (b) deep window reveals with sills, and (c) the stepped gable coping treads — these are the >10 cm features that give this quay its off-specular return and they read from every camera angle. Brick bond and mortar joints stay as the 5 mm roughness number; meshing them would be wrong physics. The gable steps in particular are a strong retroreflective set at grazing incidence across the water, which matters for any link on the Korenlei side.

CLUTTER, do not get this wrong: fronting_street is highway=pedestrian, car_access=none. There are no vehicles on Graslei. Populate instead with cafe terrace furniture on the sett quay, mooring bollards and the quay edge drop to the water, bicycles against the facade, and pedestrians. A parked-car rule applied here would be the same failure as the medieval-square case.

CONFIDENCE: macro (storey banding, gable-fronted massing, brick-with-stone-banding) is well supported by data plus row context; everything at opening and reveal scale is regional prior for restored C17 Ghent quay houses and would be overturned by a single street photograph.

reading.identification: A modest two-storey-plus-attic brick mid-terrace dwelling of the Ghent historic core, probably 18th-19th century in its present facade, fronting a sett-paved pedestrian lane behind the Graslei quay and in residential use.
reading.notes:
Set A resolves nothing on this building. The only well-resolved facade in the frame (pale, legible window rows, top centre) is a neighbour further up the block, NOT the outlined target; inside the magenta box the Google tiles have collapsed into a melted purple-grey mass with a few pinkish planar streaks. I can assert "pitched, not flat" and no more, so the roof is marked inferred despite set A nominally being the roof view. Every field here is inferred.

Storeys: 9.2 m read as total height to ridge. Ground 3.2 + one upper 2.9 puts eaves at ~6.1 m, leaving 3.1 m of roof over a 3.75 m half-span = ~40 deg pitch, the standard Flemish tiled figure. Reading 9.2 as eaves height would force three storeys and make the building taller than it reads against its neighbours in the plate. Count excludes the attic per schema.

Roof orientation is derived from the measured footprint, not from the image: a 10.3 m frontage on a 7.5 m depth cannot carry a street-facing gable, which is the narrow-and-deep typology. Ridge runs parallel to the lane; party gables into the neighbours on both sides (3 attached).

This is deliberately NOT read as a Graslei/Korenlei quay guild house. Those are narrow-fronted (5-8 m), deep, tall and gable-to-water with stepped or crow gables. The measured record here is wide, shallow and low, which is a back-lane terrace unit. Applying the quay-front stepped-gable prior would have been the generic-plausible error.

Ground floor: car_access=none on a sett path, plain building=house, no shop tag, 7 m off a side lane. The cafe glazing of this quarter belongs to the quay frontage, not to this unit.

Materials: brick relief and mortar joints are in the 1-10 cm regime and are carried entirely by roughness_mm ~5 (hand-moulded Flemish brick, fairly flush lime joints), never as mesh. Trim coded "marble" as the closest available dielectric match (eps' ~7, dense calcite) for Belgian blue limestone (arduin) used at sills, plinth and door surround; it is not literally marble. Explicit geometry requested is confined to the >10 cm regime: shallow window reveals, sills, eaves cornice.

Clutter guidance for the generator: car_access=none, so place NO vehicles on this frontage. Sett-paved pedestrian lane in the Ghent core supports leaning bicycles, wheelie bins, and a doorstep threshold stone. Detail budget should sit on the openings, the eaves line and the ground-floor door; the rear and party walls are occluded by 3 attached neighbours and deserve almost nothing.

reading.identification: A very small heritage stone house on Pensmarkt, Ghent — one of the late-medieval tripe-market houses built against the flank of the Groot Vleeshuis, 3.8 m frontage on a 13 m² plot, rough Tournai-limestone rubble walls with arched leaded-light windows, now in café use (Het Spijker) with a terrace at ground level.
reading.notes: Plate A (Google 3D tiles) is degenerate at this range — a melted mass with no facade information; nothing was read from it. Street photo _1 outlines a distant red-brick crow-stepped gable across the square that contradicts _0 and does not match a 13 m² Pensmarkt unit; treated as a geolocation error and discarded. All facade reading comes from _0. Wall is Tournai bluestone rubble, not brick — 'marble' is the closest available dielectric proxy for dense limestone (concrete would under-state permittivity); roughness 12 mm carries the irregular rubble faces and deeply raked joints in the 1–10 cm regime rather than as mesh. 'trim' = wood for the substantial dark timber joinery: window frames, leaded casements and the panelled aprons under the first-floor sills; the reveals and sills themselves are dressed stone, same as wall. Reveal class deep is supported — the wall is a thick rubble wall and jamb shadow is unambiguous in _0. Bay count is inferred: the photo shows the rhythm across the whole terrace of houses but the outline is an axis-aligned box over an obliquely-viewed facade, so I cannot isolate this unit's party walls; 2 bays follows from 3.8 m frontage minus piers with ~1.2 m openings. Roof inferred: gable-to-street on a narrow deep plot (5.4 m depth), ridge perpendicular — not visible from the pavement in either photo. Height 9.0 m is flagged no-data upstream; 3.2 + 2.6 + 2.6 = 8.4 m of storey plus roof is consistent with it and I have not overridden it. Scene direction: pedestrian street, car_access none — place no vehicles. Real clutter here is terrace furniture (stacked green chairs, round tables, umbrella), parked bicycles, blackboard menus, terracotta window planters, projecting bracket signs and enamel brewery plaques; all above 10 cm and worth explicit geometry given the 0.1 m standoff from the corridor.

reading.identification: A tall narrow brick quayside house on the Graslei/Vleeshuistragel corner in Ghent, late-Gothic/Flemish-Renaissance in idiom and restored, with a crow-stepped gable and oculus facing the Leie, natural-stone cross windows, and a tea-room occupying the quay-level ground floor.
reading.notes:
CORNER BUILDING - read the two faces differently. Gable front (9.3 m) faces the Leie/Graslei and carries all the ornament; the 16.5 m flank down Vleeshuistragel is plainer, large brick field with isolated cross windows, the VLEESHUIS street sign and the Callisto board. Bays and ridge orientation below are set against the GABLE FRONT: ridge_parallel_to_street=false means the ridge runs into the plot, i.e. parallel to Vleeshuistragel, perpendicular to the Graslei face. Do not flip this.

ROOF: stepped_gable chosen over gabled because the crow steps with projecting stone copings are the silhouette and are >10 cm relief - they must be geometry, not a painted profile. Steep tiled pitch behind, ~49 deg, derived from 5.4 m of gable above a 12.3 m eaves; B_1 shows a pitch consistent with that. Oculus/roundel and volute scrollwork in the gable head are ornament: 1-10 cm regime, roughness only, do not mesh.

CORNICE: true, but it is a corbelled brick eaves band with a painted fascia and gutter along the flank plus the stone step copings on the gable - not a classical moulded cornice. Model it as a shallow projecting band, ~0.15 m, not a bracketed entablature.

WINDOWS: stone mullion-and-transom cross windows (kruiskozijn) with leaded small-pane upper lights and red-painted joinery, clearly resolved in both photographs. Upper-floor openings on the gable front group into wide multi-light bands; 1.5 m is the single-cross-window module, use it as the unit and let the generator group two of them in the centre bays. reveal_class=deep is read from the oblique view in B_0, where the stone jamb sides and the set-back glazing plane are visible on the flank windows; wall is thick handmade brick, so ~0.25 m is right. This is the single most valuable geometric feature on the building at 28 GHz.

BALCONIES: two distinct ones on the gable front, seen - a semicircular wrought-iron balcony with potted plants at the upper level and a red-balustraded one below, plus a canted oriel with a curved metal canopy over the ground floor. All are real projecting geometry and should be built.

GROUND FLOOR: cafe_glazing. Tea-room with awning, glazed openings under segmental brick arches, and a terrace of tables and red chairs on the quay in both photographs, with a stone arch at quay level. Note the quay sits below the Graslei/tragel level - there are steps and a retaining wall; the cafe floor is the lower level.

MATERIAL: trim=marble is a stand-in for Balegem-type calcareous limestone (sills, mullions, window surrounds, gable copings) - marble is the closest calcareous stone in the library and the dielectric fit is acceptable; it is not actual marble. roughness_mm=6 is an inference, not a measurement: old handmade brick with irregular courses and deep raked/eroded joints, as seen at close range in B_0. The seen mark on this block covers wall material and trim material, which are unambiguous; the number itself is derived. Same caveat on the storeys block - the count of 4 is seen, the 3.6/2.9 m heights are back-solved from the 17.7 m datum and the observed rhythm.

CLUTTER, and please read this: fronting_street is a 2.4 m gravel tragel with car_access=none. No parked or moving vehicles anywhere near this building - this is exactly the square-full-of-cars failure. What belongs is cafe terrace furniture (tables, stacked chairs, parasols, A-boards, chalkboards), the steel quay railing and steps, bins, bikes leaning at the Graslei end, and moss/damp staining on the lower quay wall.

DETAIL BUDGET: spend it on the gable front and the first 6-8 m of the flank nearest the corner, which is what the corridor illuminates. The far end of the 16.5 m flank and the rear can stay coarse.

reading.identification: A very narrow (5.2 m) gable-fronted brick quayside house of the Flemish 16th–17th century burgher/guild-house type, wedged as a sliver infill in the Graslei/Korenlei terrace, with a horeca ground floor facing the pedestrian sett quay and dwelling/storage above.
reading.notes:
PLATE UNUSABLE. The Google 3D tiles in this region have degenerated into smeared shards; no storey line, opening, reveal or ground-floor edge survives, and the mauve cast is tile atmosphere rather than true colour. A reddish pitched-roof mass sits near the top of the magenta box but cannot be attributed to the target versus the row behind, so even the roof is marked inferred. Nothing here is seen.

TAG CAVEAT: osm building=roof. I have read this as a roof-only mapping over a real narrow house rather than as an open canopy — a 13.2 m open canopy on a 19 m2 plot with 4 attached neighbours is not a form that occurs in this terrace. If the generator honours building=roof literally it will produce a wall-less shed and should override this grammar; flagged for the data owner.

HEIGHT CONSISTENCY: 3.6 ground + 2 x 2.8 upper = 9.2 m eaves, + ~4.0 m stepped gable = the given 13.2 m. Storey count 3 is derived from that budget, not observed. If the 13.2 m turns out to be eaves rather than ridge, go to 4 storeys and keep the gable.

CLUTTER: fronting way is highway=path, surface=sett, car_access=none. NO VEHICLES on this frontage — this is the pedestrian quay, and a parked-car rule firing here would repeat the medieval-square failure. Populate with cafe terrace furniture and parasols against the ground-floor glazing, bollards, bike clusters, and the quay edge with moored boats. Sett surface should be a roughness parameter, not tessellated cobbles.

DETAIL BUDGET: concentrate on the gable silhouette (the crow-steps are the feature a rotated camera judges, and they are genuine >10 cm geometry producing strong edge diffraction against sky), on the window reveals and sills, and on the ground-floor glazing plane. The two flanks are buried between four attached neighbours, receive no beam and should get near-zero budget.

PHYSICS: brick relief and lime mortar joints at 5-8 mm stay as the 6 mm RMS roughness number plus a scattering coefficient, never as mesh. The 0.12 m window reveals, the sills, the string courses and the gable steps are the facets that matter and must be explicit geometry. Trim is set to concrete as the nearest available dielectric proxy for Balegem sandstone (the real trim material, eps ~4-6); marble in the enum would be too high. No cornice: gable-fronted houses of this type terminate in the stepped coping rather than an eaves cornice, and the string courses stand in for the sandstone/brick banding (speklagen). No balconies — absent from this building type in Ghent.

CONFIDENCE 0.35 reflects zero usable imagery plus an ambiguous building tag. The grammar is a defensible instance of the type, not a recovery of this specific facade. A single street photograph would move most of these fields to seen and roughly double the confidence.
